intro: The real people Noble met on his voyage — shipmates, governors, a dispossessed king, and the potentates of China. 'Read' is where each appears in the reader; 'Editor's note' adds context the 1748 book leaves out.

people.name: Charles Frederick Noble
people.role: Author; officer in the East India Company's service
people.book: The preface promises the 'genuine production of a real traveller, an officer in the service of the East India Company… an accurate observer, who describes chiefly what he has seen.'
people.note: Beyond this one journey little is recorded of Noble himself — the book is almost all we know. 'Captain Charles Frederick Noble' appears on the title page; his promised value lies in being, as he stresses, an eyewitness rather than an armchair compiler.

people.name: The King of Madura
people.role: Dethroned monarch of the island of Madura
people.book: Fled his own island when the Dutch deposed him, escaped their pursuers, and threw himself on the protection of the English ship Onslow — only to be 'tragically delivered' back to the Dutch amid a scene Noble calls one of the most melancholy ever acted in the East.
people.note: Madura, off the north coast of Java, had long been a vassal of the Dutch East India Company (VOC). Noble's account — of a king pleading for help and the crew weeping as he was led away — is a striking contemporary indictment of both Dutch 'insolence and barbarity' and 'English pusillanimity and misconduct.'

people.name: Captain Congreve
people.book: The English captain who first sheltered the fleeing King of Madura, was imprisoned by the Sultan of Benjar, and was ultimately powerless when the Dutch demanded the king's surrender.
people.note: The 'Onslow' was an East Indiaman (an English Company trading ship). Noble's account shows how thin English protection could be in the waters the Dutch Company dominated — even a captain could end up in a native sultan's prison.

people.name: The Sultan of Benjar
people.role: Ruler on Borneo who imprisoned Capt. Congreve
people.book: The sovereign to whom the trading port of Benjar belonged, who clapped the English captain in prison — a glimpse of the perils of Company commerce far from any European fleet.
people.note: Benjar is Banjarmasin, on the south coast of Borneo — a pepper port contested between Dutch and English traders in the 18th century.

people.name: The Female Volunteer
people.role: A woman who slipped aboard ship
people.book: 'A Female volunteer gets aboard, but discovered' — one of the book's earliest and most human curiosities, a woman managing to reach the outward-bound vessel during the press at Gravesend.
people.note: The Thames 'press' of men for outward East-Indiamen was unruly, and the occasional woman did manage to smuggle herself aboard. Noble's passing mention is a small gem of social history.

people.name: The Emperor of China
people.role: Sovereign of the Empire of China
people.book: Noble describes the emperor's title, his palace and throne at Pekin, his person and dress, and the ceremonial manner of receiving ambassadors.
people.note: In 1747–48 the Dragon Throne was held by the Qianlong Emperor — one of the longest-reigning and most powerful monarchs in world history, who received no embassy from the English until 1793. Noble's account reflects what a merchant saw of that grand and distant court.

people.name: The Governor of Batavia
people.role: Chief magistrate of the Dutch capital at Batavia
people.book: Noble dwells on 'the grandeur of its governor,' the state and ceremony with which the head of the Dutch settlement at Batavia kept court.
people.note: The Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies ruled from Batavia (modern Jakarta) what was arguably the richest corporation-state on earth — a private company with fleets, armies and provinces.
